subject: fixed.x again: Are two models equivalent or not?

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: fixed.x again: Are two models equivalent or not?
parts:
I am thinking about a scenario related to the previous discussion on fixed vs. random
manifest exogenous variables (https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/69H6ax6upMc/m/oRrML3gWAwAJ).
As shown below, the default option of fixed.x = TRUE (also used in Mplus) can lead
two models being equivalent on some fit measures but not equivalent on some other
measures. (This example is different from a previous one because fixed.x = TRUE
is used on both models.)

Let us assume that a researcher is examining two simple path models with four observed
variables. The researcher agrees with the default value of fixed.x in lavaan and so
makes no change for this argument.

(I used HolzingerSwineford1939 just for convenience. Some of the phenomena found
below are not specific to this dataset.)
library(lavaan)
#> This is lavaan 0.6-15
#> lavaan is FREE software! Please report any bugs.
dat <- HolzingerSwineford1939

mod1 <-
"
x2 ~ x1
x3 ~ x2 + x1
x4 ~ x3
"

mod2 <-
"
x3 ~ x2 + x1
x4 ~ x3
"
These two models are sometimes considered equivalent (in terms of implied covariance
matrix). The only difference is the relation between x2 and x1. In mod1, x2 is
predicted by x1. In mod2, x2 and x1 just covary. Let's assume that both are theoretically
possible. Also assume that the variables x1, x2, x3, and x4 are multivariate normal in
the population. They are fitted in lavaan using the default options:
fit1 <- sem(mod1, dat)
fit2 <- sem(mod2, dat)

fit1
#> lavaan 0.6.15 ended normally after 1 iteration
#> 
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                         7
#> 
#>   Number of observations                           301
#> 
#> Model Test User Model:
#>                                                       
#>   Test statistic                                38.132
#>   Degrees of freedom                                 2
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000
fit2
#> lavaan 0.6.15 ended normally after 1 iteration
#> 
#>   Estimator                                         ML
#>   Optimization method                           NLMINB
#>   Number of model parameters                         5
#> 
#>   Number of observations                           301
#> 
#> Model Test User Model:
#>                                                       
#>   Test statistic                                38.132
#>   Degrees of freedom                                 2
#>   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000

These two models have identical model degrees of freedom (2) and identical model chi-square.
This is expected and is necessarily true, regardless of the data. From this perspective, they are
equivalent models.

However, they do not have the same number of free model parameters. In mod1, only x1
is treated as fixed. In mod2, both x1 and x2 are treated as fixed. Therefore, the number of
free parameters are different (7 in mod1, and 5 in mod2).

These are the fit measures:

round(cbind(fit1 = fitMeasures(fit1),
            fit2 = fitMeasures(fit2)), 3)
#>                            fit1     fit2
#> npar                      7.000    5.000
#> fmin                      0.063    0.063
#> chisq                    38.132   38.132
#> df                        2.000    2.000
#> pvalue                    0.000    0.000
#> baseline.chisq          157.076  129.212
#> baseline.df               6.000    5.000
#> baseline.pvalue           0.000    0.000
#> cfi                       0.761    0.709
#> tli                       0.282    0.273
#> nnfi                      0.282    0.273
#> rfi                       0.272    0.262
#> nfi                       0.757    0.705
#> pnfi                      0.252    0.282
#> ifi                       0.767    0.716
#> rni                       0.761    0.709
#> logl                  -1352.285 -890.448
#> unrestricted.logl     -1333.219 -871.382
#> aic                    2718.570 1790.897
#> bic                    2744.520 1809.432
#> ntotal                  301.000  301.000
#> bic2                   2722.320 1793.575
#> rmsea                     0.245    0.245
#> rmsea.ci.lower            0.181    0.181
#> rmsea.ci.upper            0.316    0.316
#> rmsea.ci.level            0.900    0.900
#> rmsea.pvalue              0.000    0.000
#> rmsea.close.h0            0.050    0.050
#> rmsea.notclose.pvalue     1.000    1.000
#> rmsea.notclose.h0         0.080    0.080
#> rmr                       0.137    0.137
#> rmr_nomean                0.137    0.137
#> srmr                      0.101    0.101
#> srmr_bentler              0.101    0.101
#> srmr_bentler_nomean       0.101    0.101
#> crmr                      0.130    0.130
#> crmr_nomean               0.130    0.130
#> srmr_mplus                0.101    0.101
#> srmr_mplus_nomean         0.101    0.101
#> cn_05                    48.294   48.294
#> cn_01                    73.702   73.702
#> gfi                       0.928    0.898
#> agfi                      0.641    0.491
#> pgfi                      0.186    0.180
#> mfi                       0.942    0.942
#> ecvi                      0.173    0.160
For most measures of "absolute fit", e.g., RMSEA, SRMR, RMR, the
two models have exactly identical fit, which is expected.

However, for the measures of incremental fit, e.g., CFI and TLI, mod1
(with x2 predicted by x1) has better fit than mod2. This is because they
do not have the same baseline model under fixed.x = TRUE.

Suppose the researcher compares the two models on AIC and BIC ...
mod2 is preferred because it has lower values. This is because mod2
has fewer model parameters, even though both models have exactly the
same model chi-squares and model degrees of freedom. AIC and BIC
are usually not used in this case but I also see no reason why they
cannot be used (please correct me if I am wrong).

The argument for setting fixed.x = TRUE, applied to mod1 and mod2
separately, would lead to different numbers of parameters. If mod1 and mod2
are proposed and tested by two independent researchers, then everything
seems fine with fixed.x = TRUE.

However, when mod1 and mod2 are examined together, how should we
handle fixed.x?

Using the default, with x1 treated as fixed in mod1, while x1 and x2 treated
as fixed in mod2?

Manually treating only x1 as fixed in both models because it is the only variable
which is exogenous in both models?

Using fixed.x = FALSE in both models?

Note that the decision affects not only measures of incremental fit, but
also affects SEs and CIs in the standardized solution.

Regards,
Shu Fai Cheung (張樹輝)

P.S.: Although the discussion above is on the fixed.x argument, this issue
is not unique to lavaan because, as far as I know, Mplus also does what
"fixed.x = TRUE" does, except for a case discussed before in this group
before (MLR and missing data).

messages.subject: Re: fixed.x again: Are two models equivalent or not?
parts:
Hi Shu Fai,
I suppose that one way of approaching your question is through the threefold distinction that I have proposed between three kinds of model equivalence.  Very roughly:
Statistical equivalence: Different syntax produces same fit.
Syntactical equivalence: Same syntax but different interpretations.
Semantic equivalence:  Different syntax but same interpretation.

It seems to me that the results you describe feel paradoxical if we implicitly assume that statistical equivalence implies semantic equivalence.  If you Model 1 and Model 2 are just two ways of representing the same thing, then we expect identical fit from every measure.  However, on reflection, I think that we have reason to question this implication.  Model 1 seeks to explain x2 whereas Model 2 does not.  In this way the models differ semantically despite being equivalent statistically.

This is also related to what I said on SEMNET about fit being a multi-dimensional construct.  So, it should not bother us when measures of different aspects of fit behave differently from one another.

The goal of comparative fit indices is to evaluate whether the free parameters explain enough of the covariance structure (and perhaps mean structure) to be worth estimating.  The difference in semantics makes this a different question for Model 1 than for Model 2.  Model 1 tries to explain more of the covariance structure (the covariance between x1 and x2) than does Model 2.  This raises the bar for x1, leading to different baseline models and different comparative fit indices.  (However, one could use a custom baseline model if one wished to compare them using the same baseline for each.)

One might argue that on the basis of the difference in interpretation, one should a priori prefer Model 1 to Model 2, and so if the fit is a wash, one should already lean toward Model 1.  However, if the models otherwise fit well and the association between x1 and x2 were within sampling error of zero, then one might prefer a model that omitted this association, it would not be worth modeling.

In sum, I do not think that we should expect the same fixed.x comparative fit for these models just because their absolute fit is statistically equivalent.  However, if for some reason we wanted to orchestrate a comparison of comparative fit between them, we could do that by using the same baseline model for each.  In a sense, the difference in comparative fit indices is doing its job by reminding us that the models differ semantically despite their statistical equivalence.

Keith

Markus, K. A. (2008). Hypothesis formulation, model interpretation, and model equivalence: Implications of a mereological causal interpretation of structural equation models. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 43, 177-209.

Markus, K. A. (2002).  Statistical equivalence, semantic equivalence, eliminative induction, and the Raykov-Marcoulides proof of infinite equivalence. Structural Equation Modeling, 9, 503-522.

messages.author: bc810b1d0900407f
messages.subject: Re: fixed.x again: Are two models equivalent or not?
parts:
Dear Keith,

Many many thanks for your detailed comments and the two references.

That scenario came to me based on something I observed in working with others and teaching. Two options are involved, the fixed.x option and the choice of the baseline model, which can be affected by which variables are treated as fixed. I have no strong preference on what should be done, e.g., fixed or random. They need to be determined case by case.

However, for lavaan, Mplus, and Amos, from my experience, some users are not aware of the existence of these two options, and the default behaviors of the SEM program they use. Kline (2023) added a box (Box 9.2) on the fixed.x option (Bollen, 1989, also covered this topic but focused on the distributional assumptions needed for ML, not on the settings in SEM programs), and also used several paragraphs to discuss the choice of the baseline models (not new, as they were already in previous editions). I am not sure how much these two options are covered in other introductory textbooks on SEM. Researchers may just use the default of an SEM program, and they may never notice that the options have already been involved in determining their results until they encounter scenarios like the one I present and the one you presented in an earlier post, or for some reasons fit the same model using two SEM programs and found some difference in the results.

I do not have any suggestions. Maybe always state in the output of summary() which variables, if any, are treated as fixed variables? Always report in the output of summary() the baseline model used for CFI and similar incremental fit measures?

-- Shu Fai

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: fixed.x again: Are two models equivalent or not?
parts:
Shu Fai,
Thanks for reminding me that fixed x is discussed by Bollen 1989.  I had completely forgotten about that.

I agree that there is probably some need to raise awareness now that this option has become readily available and sometimes the default.

I do not think that there is any question that the two models meet the definition for statistical equivalence.  The "fit" in the definition refers only to the value of the fit function being minimized (and thus chi-square derived from it using only properties of the data).  It should not be interpreted to refer to any possible fit index.  If we think of the target model and the data as a tuple, then statistically equivalent models will share the same fit for any fit measure which is an intrinsic property of this tuple.  Comparative fit indices are not intrinsic properties of this tuple because they depend essentially on the choice of baseline model which cannot be derived from the tuple and introduces new information.  Any such non-intrisic aspects of fit cannot be considered as 'fit' as the term is used in the definition of statistical equivalence.  If that door were left open, there would be no statistically equivalent models and the term would loose its value.

I would welcome some additional default summary output that gives the number of observed moments used to test the model, the number of free parameters left after excluding those impacted by fixed.x,  and perhaps the number of each excluded by fixed.x (which should always be the same for each).  Such output would certainly make fixed.x easier to teach by allowing the user to readily verify the expected result of using fixed.x.

Keith
